The inverse design method prescribes desired distributions of angle of attack (α) and axial induction factor (a) along the blade span.
The Trust-Region-Reflective (TRF) optimization method is used to iterate on the blade geometry (twist and chord) to match the prescribed α and a distributions.
The TRF method is found to be more stable than the multi-dimensional Newton iteration method in constrained blade design problems.
The inverse design method is demonstrated for conventional single-rotor horizontal axis wind turbines and then extended to dual-rotor wind turbines.
The effect of the spinning blades on the airflow is modeled using the Actuator Disk Method (ADM), which introduces body forces in the Navier-Stokes equations.
The computational setup uses a uniform, smooth inflow, assumes all rotor blades are identical, and investigates only mean (time-steady) performance.
A mesh sensitivity study is performed, and a grid resolution of 101x229 cells is found to be sufficient for the RANS/ADM solver.
The inverse design algorithm is tested on three different single-rotor wind turbine cases, including the Betz optimum rotor and the NREL 5 MW turbine.
The algorithm is able to successfully reproduce the original blade geometry (twist and chord distributions) for the NREL 5 MW turbine case.
When the desired α and a distributions are prescribed using the BEM method, the inverse design algorithm can still yield a blade geometry consistent with the RANS/ADM direct solver.
The inverse design method is general and can be applied to wind turbines with an arbitrary number of rotor disks, not just dual-rotor configurations.
Manufacturing and transportation constraints on conventional wind turbine blades can lead to aerodynamically sub-optimal designs in the blade root region.
Dual-rotor wind turbines can efficiently harness energy from the blade root region and enhance wake mixing to reduce wake losses.
The inverse design methodology presented in this paper is a computationally efficient approach to explore blade designs that maximize wake mixing.
The use of RANS CFD in the inverse design process allows for the exploration of designs that can better model turbulent wake mixing compared to potential flow methods.
